title: Optimizing VHF Repeater Coordination Using Cluster Analysis

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 2 is the title page with a centered footer number; normal headers and Page 1 of 51 through Page 51 of 51 otherwise identify the physical sequence.

notes: All 51 text pages and all 51 rendered pages were reviewed in order by the root thread; independent read-only audits separately covered pages 1-17, 18-34, and 35-51.

The root used seven full-range JPEG contact proxies and one formula crop, each below 450000 bytes. Independent audits used fresh bounded contexts. Original 180-DPI PNGs remained on disk and no further image was added after the root's eight-proxy context ceiling.

Text extraction is complete but corrupts several symbols; visual review confirmed flow arrows, roots, plus/minus signs, Greek symbols, table structure, graph topology, colors, MATLAB tilde syntax, and physical code cropping.

context_sources.summary: The official VHF repeater problem supplies domain, spectrum, offset, tone, user, scale, and terrain constraints.
Radio-technology references motivate repeater separation, antenna height, and CTCSS gating.
Eleven references cover repeaters, radio horizon, CTCSS, k-means, MATLAB, propagation, and amateur-radio coordination.

inputs: potential user coordinates inside a radius-40-mile region
145-148 MHz band, plus-or-minus 600 kHz offsets, nominal channel width, and 54 CTCSS tones
k, d_s, h_r, d_h, d_p, l_n, l_c, and synthetic city or rural distributions
outputs: CTCSS repeater positions and long-distance/local tone lines
plus/minus parity labels and connectivity plots
open, CTCSS, nominal channel, and served-user counts
sensitivity tables and qualitative terrain guidance
decisions: which heuristic to use for infrastructure count versus claimed connectivity
where to place open and tone-gated repeaters
how many towers and tones are required in each case
when a minimum or terrain claim must be withheld

section_map.summary: The Abstract frames the 40-mile, 145-148 MHz repeater-coordination task, introduces the Bender Snaking and Branching heuristics, names city and rural synthetic cases, contrasts repeater counts and connectivity, and announces 10,000-user and mountainous-terrain extensions.

The title page and two contents pages expose the complete argument from restatement and assumptions through two algorithms, matched city and rural cases, stress and sensitivity sections, conclusion, full-page plots, and two MATLAB appendices.

The restatement retains the 40-mile radius, 145-148 MHz band, plus-or-minus 600 kHz offsets, 54 CTCSS tones, 1,000 simultaneous users, a 10,000-user extension, and mountainous terrain as the exact decision envelope.

The assumptions define a planar closed system with no external interference, isotropic antennas, homogeneous compliant users, fixed user range, Euclidean geometry, and a coordination-distance interpretation before stating why each simplification permits the two placement heuristics.

The technology section serves as the engineering introduction: it explains repeater separation, coverage overlap, antenna-height range, and CTCSS activation, then converts those mechanisms into spacing, tower-height, channel, and tone constraints used by both models.

Figure 1 and the prose describe k-means population clusters, a highest-coverage starting point, perimeter growth toward valuable clusters, conditional CTCSS placement when channel deficit is positive, and optional reclustering.

The mathematical interpretation defines n, k, d_s, h_r, d_h, Delta f, N_c, N_f, O, and D; Algorithms 1 and 2 search candidate CTCSS angles and open-repeater cluster directions until at least 1,000 users have channels.

Figure 2 and the Branching prose create an open backbone, repeatedly recluster remaining users, extend branches from the nearest existing network node, then add long-distance and local CTCSS lines after coverage construction.

The Branching mathematical section adds l_n and l_c, selects a distant or high-value target, places d_h-spaced nodes, reclusters uncovered users, attaches branches, and uses Algorithm 3 plus long-distance CTCSS chains to recover channel capacity and connectivity.

The comparison section uses parallel similarities and differences: both models use k-means and frequency-offset parity, while Snaking grows one continuous path and inserts CTCSS during growth whereas Branching builds a backbone, reclusters every branch, and adds tones afterward.

The city case defines a central high-density population surface, explains plus/minus parity, and establishes the common parameter and symbol conventions needed to compare the two layouts on the same synthetic geography.

The matched city and rural results preserve both methods under each synthetic geography: city Snaking 9 open plus 8 CTCSS, city Branching 9 plus 17, rural Snaking 10 plus 8 with 1,080 covered users, and rural Branching 8 plus 17, together with placement narratives and tone allocation.

The four parity and CTCSS diagrams test post-placement graph consequences: odd cycles and adjacent same-sign nodes expose leakage, while Branching uses tones 1-3 for long-distance paths and 4-8 locally but never quantifies its claimed connectivity advantage.

The scale section draws 12,000 potential users, reduces channel spacing from 25 to 10 kHz, applies the existing heuristic to connect 10,000 users, and reports 19 open and 33 CTCSS repeaters while printing an inconsistent total of 42.

The mountainous-terrain section offers a qualitative placement rule for single peaks, multiple peaks, mountain chains, foothills, and valleys, but does not add a DEM, propagation computation, or experiment to the algorithm.

The sensitivity section varies cluster count, open-repeater separation and implied tower height, and initial potential population, then reports repeater counts and qualitative cost tradeoffs while omitting repeated seeds and several plotted settings.
The final evaluation labels adaptability and dynamic reclustering as strengths and records k-means dependence and last-user search as weaknesses before the conclusion opens.

The conclusion compares the four exact case totals, describes Snaking as lower-infrastructure and Branching as better connected, claims an absolute minimum of 17 without a lower bound, and comments on remaining CTCSS lines.

The references and Appendix A preserve 11 sources and seven full-page city, rural, CTCSS, and 10,000-user layouts so node classes, coverage circles, parity, tone labels, and spatial connectivity can be inspected at full scale.

Appendix B supplies 319 lines of Snaking MATLAB and 500 lines of Branching MATLAB, exposing parameter initialization, k-means calls, angle search, user deletion, channel accounting, long-distance tone chains, plotting, hard-coded paths, commented blocks, and implementation defects.

assumptions.summary: The circular service region can be represented as a flat Euclidean plane.
The designed repeater network is closed and experiences no outside interference.
Repeater and user antennas are isotropic so communication regions can be drawn as circles.
Users have equal low-power equipment, follow operating rules, and are homogeneous for placement purposes.
A user can communicate with any repeater within a fixed distance d_s.
At least ten miles of coordination separation is a useful general repeater-spacing rule.
The printed antenna-height rule adequately links tower height to service distance.
CTCSS tones create separable logical service lines and can be counted as additional capacity.
K-means centers and neighborhood population counts identify valuable placement directions.
The first open repeater should be near the candidate covering the most potential users.
Each nominal frequency can serve one simultaneous user under N_f=min(N_c,O).
A finite angular grid is sufficient to locate the best CTCSS candidate.
Alternating open and CTCSS placement will eventually frequency-serve at least 1,000 users.
A high-value backbone followed by dynamic reclustering improves network connectivity.
High-density locations can be connected by shared long-distance CTCSS lines and supplemented locally.
Alternating plus/minus 600 kHz labels is an adequate post-placement frequency plan.
One city and one rural synthetic distribution are representative tests of the two heuristics.
Narrowing channel width from 25 kHz to 10 kHz is a valid way to scale nominal capacity.
Mountain effects can be handled through qualitative placement near peaks, foothills, and valleys.
Single runs at selected k, d_h, and potential-population values reveal parameter sensitivity.

results_trace.summary: City Snaking uses 9 open and 8 CTCSS repeaters for 17 total.
City Branching uses 9 open and 17 CTCSS repeaters for 26 total.
Rural Snaking uses 10 open and 8 CTCSS repeaters for 18 total and reports 1,080 covered users.
Rural Branching uses 8 open and 17 CTCSS repeaters for 25 total.
The 10,000-user case reports 19 open and 33 CTCSS repeaters but incorrectly prints a total of 42 instead of 52.

writing_logic.summary: Abstract chain: official repeater task -> two named heuristics -> city and rural cases -> infrastructure/connectivity comparison -> 10,000-user and terrain extension.
Opening chain: problem resources and targets -> explicit assumptions -> available repeater and CTCSS mechanisms.
Snaking chain: intuitive flow chart -> k-means and variable table -> coverage/channel equations -> Algorithms 1 and 2 -> 1,000-user stop.
Branching chain: backbone flow chart -> added long-distance variables -> far/high-value target -> dynamic branch attachment -> tone-line augmentation.
Comparison chain: shared clustering and parity -> continuous path versus backbone/branches -> when tones are added -> infrastructure/connectivity tradeoff.
City chain: population surface and parity rule -> Snaking parameters, placement, count, parity -> Branching placement, tones, count, parity.
Rural chain: separated towns -> Snaking coverage/count/parity -> Branching backbone/tone allocation/count/parity.
Extension chain: 10,000-user channel narrowing and count -> qualitative terrain placement -> parameter sensitivity.
Evaluation chain: labeled strengths -> labeled weaknesses -> exact four-case totals -> claimed minimum and connectivity conclusion.
Evidence appendix chain: references -> full-page plots for every principal case -> complete Snaking and Branching MATLAB listings.
Code chain: parameter initialization -> clustering -> candidate generation -> coverage deletion -> channel update -> plotting and printed counts.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: An abstract that names two mechanisms and matched cases plausibly improves judge traceability, but does not prove the minimum claim.
A parallel comparison section plausibly helps a judge see infrastructure-versus-connectivity tradeoffs before inspecting figures.
Supplying source code plausibly improves transparency, although defects and missing inputs prevent reproducibility.

weaknesses.summary: The paper operationalizes the 1,000-user requirement as selecting and connecting 1,000 users from a larger potential population rather than modeling 1,000 simultaneous transmissions with duration and interference.
The closed-system, no-external-interference, isotropic-antenna, homogeneous-user, and fixed-range assumptions remove major radio and behavioral mechanisms without a sensitivity or fallback model.
The printed distance-in-miles equals sqrt(1.5 A_f) relation is physically questionable and differs in form from common radio-horizon rules; no calibration data are supplied.
The prose mixes a ten-mile coordination separation with d_h values of 15 or 20 miles and overlapping coverage circles without a single explicit semantic distinction.
CTCSS tones gate receivers but are not independent RF channels; the paper repeatedly treats tone count, channel count, and simultaneous capacity as interchangeable resources.
Algorithm inputs use d_p for CTCSS placement even though the main Snaking parameter table defines d_s and d_h but not d_p.
The printed user-to-repeater distance relation has a subtraction between squared coordinate differences; this can make the radicand negative and contradicts Euclidean distance.
O=3/Delta f divides the full three-megahertz band by nominal channel width without duplex pairing, guard bands, occupied bandwidth, adjacent-channel interference, or coordination rules.
N_f=min(N_c,O) assumes one simultaneous user per nominal channel and omits transmission duration, spatial reuse, contention, and interference.
Algorithm 1 scores remaining users near a CTCSS candidate even though adding a tone-gated repeater does not by itself extend connectivity of the open network.
Algorithms 1 and 2 mix zero-based and one-based intervals such as [0,k] and [1,k], and several candidate counters are not explicitly initialized.
The Branching prose says the backbone connects the two highest-scoring clusters, while Algorithm 3 selects the farthest cluster according to phi.
Algorithm 3 defines theta as the distance between R_T and T but immediately uses theta inside cosine and sine, where it must be an angle.
After selecting the nearest existing node R_T as a branch origin, Algorithm 3 updates R_j from R_(j-1), leaving the actual branch start and indices ambiguous.
The plus/minus parity assignment is performed graphically after placement and has no general feasibility algorithm, band-edge check, or proof for graphs with cycles.
The city Snaking parity graph is an odd cycle and contains adjacent equal signs; the paper acknowledges possible signal leakage but accepts it without a quantitative frequency analysis.
The Branching model's claimed outstanding connectivity is not defined by a connectivity, latency, path-length, reliability, or robustness metric.
City and rural evaluation each use one synthetic distribution with no repeated random seeds, distributional variance, statistical test, or real coordinate validation.
The rural parity graph again contains adjacent step-up repeaters, and the proposed alternative-direction workaround is qualitative rather than a verified spectrum solution.
The 10,000-user section states 19 open plus 33 CTCSS repeaters total 42, but the arithmetic total is 52.
The conclusion says 12 of 54 CTCSS lines remain, implying 42 used, which conflicts with the reported 33 CTCSS repeaters and incomplete tone-reuse accounting.
Reducing Delta f from 25 kHz to 10 kHz is treated as automatically legal and interference-free without occupied-bandwidth, receiver-selectivity, or coordination validation.
Figure 15 and the full-page Figure 24 omit a local legend and depend on colors and shapes defined in earlier figures.
The mountainous-terrain section is purely qualitative and supplies no DEM, propagation model, shadowing calculation, asymmetric link test, optimization objective, or experiment.
The cluster-count sensitivity claims k=5,10,20 were tested, but Figure 16 displays only k=10 and k=20, and no seed variation is reported.
The reported k=20 result is 8 open plus 8 CTCSS equals 16, contradicting the later claim that 17 is the absolute minimum.

The d_h sensitivity uses 10, 15, and 20 miles with implied heights 66 ft 8 in, 150 ft, and 266 ft 8 in, but Figure 17 labels the parameter only d and no propagation validation supports the conversion.
The initial-population sensitivity table labels its first column d_h even though the entries 1400, 3000, and 10000 are potential-user counts.
Larger potential populations produce fewer open repeaters because the algorithm may choose the easiest 1,000 users, which can sacrifice geographic fairness and coverage obligations.

The conclusion calls 17 an absolute minimum although the algorithms are heuristics, no lower bound or optimality proof is given, and sensitivity cells report 16 or even 9 repeaters under changed inputs.
The statement that all 54 CTCSS lines are unnecessary lacks a complete allocation, reuse, collision, and simultaneous-capacity ledger.
The MATLAB appendices hard-code local Windows paths, domain bounds, target user counts, and plotting conventions, and provide no input package, seed, output data, or execution log.
Snaking code assigns rep(1,2)=clusters(index,1), copying the x coordinate into y for the first repeater.
Snaking initializes numclus=10 but several starting and direction loops are hard-coded over only five clusters.
Snaking scores a CTCSS candidate using reppl but appears to delete covered users using an open-repeater position, so scoring and state update may refer to different nodes.
Snaking prose uses d_h=15 while code constructs open candidates at sepdist*1.5 after initializing sepdist=10; the parameter link is implicit and brittle.
Several quadrant formulas and a branch using rep(1,1) instead of the latest repeater make the direction computation difficult to reconcile with Algorithm 2.
Boundary fallback repeatedly changes angles but does not visibly enforce a safe candidate-index or retry bound.
Branching runs kmeans on concat containing x, y, and density score, whereas the paper describes geographic x-y clustering; scale normalization is not supplied.
Branching initializes cluslongscr with numclus rows but loops over numlongdist clusters, relying on implicit array growth and inconsistent dimensions.
The nearest-neighbor long-distance CTCSS chain and indexnum==actlongdist boundary logic are heuristic and may mishandle cycle completion or self-selection.
Branching appears to index pluncovered(i) as a scalar where two coordinate columns are needed, indicating a likely coordinate bug.
Large blocks of source code are commented out with percent-brace delimiters, include debugging output and hard-coded alternatives, and do not establish which path generated the published figures.
Multiple long MATLAB lines are physically cropped at the right page edge, so parts of conditions and plotting calls cannot be recovered from either text extraction or raster review.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace the height rule and circular range assumptions with a calibrated bidirectional link budget, antenna pattern, terrain profile, fading margin, and measured coverage data.
Build an explicit duplex channel plan with occupied bandwidth, guard bands, spatial reuse, CTCSS reuse, and an interference graph before defining simultaneous capacity.
Formulate Snaking as a reproducible multi-objective heuristic with typed candidate sets, initialized counters, fair user coverage, and seed-controlled clustering.
Formulate Branching as a graph optimization with explicit backbone objective, branch origin, connectivity metric, tone-line routing, and cycle-feasible parity assignment.
Use measured or generative city and rural populations with many seeds, confidence intervals, fairness metrics, and identical comparator cases.
Integrate DEM-based propagation and shadowing into candidate reach, then validate single-peak, multi-peak, valley, and ridge cases quantitatively.
Refactor the MATLAB into parameterized functions, fix coordinate and dimension errors, recover cropped lines from original source, package inputs, set seeds, and emit machine-readable logs.

unresolved_questions: The paper operationalizes the 1,000-user requirement as selecting and connecting 1,000 users from a larger potential population rather than modeling 1,000 simultaneous transmissions with duration and interference.
The closed-system, no-external-interference, isotropic-antenna, homogeneous-user, and fixed-range assumptions remove major radio and behavioral mechanisms without a sensitivity or fallback model.
The printed distance-in-miles equals sqrt(1.5 A_f) relation is physically questionable and differs in form from common radio-horizon rules; no calibration data are supplied.
The prose mixes a ten-mile coordination separation with d_h values of 15 or 20 miles and overlapping coverage circles without a single explicit semantic distinction.
CTCSS tones gate receivers but are not independent RF channels; the paper repeatedly treats tone count, channel count, and simultaneous capacity as interchangeable resources.
Algorithm inputs use d_p for CTCSS placement even though the main Snaking parameter table defines d_s and d_h but not d_p.
The printed user-to-repeater distance relation has a subtraction between squared coordinate differences; this can make the radicand negative and contradicts Euclidean distance.
O=3/Delta f divides the full three-megahertz band by nominal channel width without duplex pairing, guard bands, occupied bandwidth, adjacent-channel interference, or coordination rules.
N_f=min(N_c,O) assumes one simultaneous user per nominal channel and omits transmission duration, spatial reuse, contention, and interference.
Algorithm 1 scores remaining users near a CTCSS candidate even though adding a tone-gated repeater does not by itself extend connectivity of the open network.
Algorithms 1 and 2 mix zero-based and one-based intervals such as [0,k] and [1,k], and several candidate counters are not explicitly initialized.
The Branching prose says the backbone connects the two highest-scoring clusters, while Algorithm 3 selects the farthest cluster according to phi.
Algorithm 3 defines theta as the distance between R_T and T but immediately uses theta inside cosine and sine, where it must be an angle.
After selecting the nearest existing node R_T as a branch origin, Algorithm 3 updates R_j from R_(j-1), leaving the actual branch start and indices ambiguous.
The plus/minus parity assignment is performed graphically after placement and has no general feasibility algorithm, band-edge check, or proof for graphs with cycles.
The city Snaking parity graph is an odd cycle and contains adjacent equal signs; the paper acknowledges possible signal leakage but accepts it without a quantitative frequency analysis.
The Branching model's claimed outstanding connectivity is not defined by a connectivity, latency, path-length, reliability, or robustness metric.
City and rural evaluation each use one synthetic distribution with no repeated random seeds, distributional variance, statistical test, or real coordinate validation.
The rural parity graph again contains adjacent step-up repeaters, and the proposed alternative-direction workaround is qualitative rather than a verified spectrum solution.
The 10,000-user section states 19 open plus 33 CTCSS repeaters total 42, but the arithmetic total is 52.
The conclusion says 12 of 54 CTCSS lines remain, implying 42 used, which conflicts with the reported 33 CTCSS repeaters and incomplete tone-reuse accounting.
Reducing Delta f from 25 kHz to 10 kHz is treated as automatically legal and interference-free without occupied-bandwidth, receiver-selectivity, or coordination validation.
Figure 15 and the full-page Figure 24 omit a local legend and depend on colors and shapes defined in earlier figures.
The mountainous-terrain section is purely qualitative and supplies no DEM, propagation model, shadowing calculation, asymmetric link test, optimization objective, or experiment.
The cluster-count sensitivity claims k=5,10,20 were tested, but Figure 16 displays only k=10 and k=20, and no seed variation is reported.
The reported k=20 result is 8 open plus 8 CTCSS equals 16, contradicting the later claim that 17 is the absolute minimum.

The d_h sensitivity uses 10, 15, and 20 miles with implied heights 66 ft 8 in, 150 ft, and 266 ft 8 in, but Figure 17 labels the parameter only d and no propagation validation supports the conversion.
The initial-population sensitivity table labels its first column d_h even though the entries 1400, 3000, and 10000 are potential-user counts.
Larger potential populations produce fewer open repeaters because the algorithm may choose the easiest 1,000 users, which can sacrifice geographic fairness and coverage obligations.

The conclusion calls 17 an absolute minimum although the algorithms are heuristics, no lower bound or optimality proof is given, and sensitivity cells report 16 or even 9 repeaters under changed inputs.
The statement that all 54 CTCSS lines are unnecessary lacks a complete allocation, reuse, collision, and simultaneous-capacity ledger.
The MATLAB appendices hard-code local Windows paths, domain bounds, target user counts, and plotting conventions, and provide no input package, seed, output data, or execution log.
Snaking code assigns rep(1,2)=clusters(index,1), copying the x coordinate into y for the first repeater.
Snaking initializes numclus=10 but several starting and direction loops are hard-coded over only five clusters.
Snaking scores a CTCSS candidate using reppl but appears to delete covered users using an open-repeater position, so scoring and state update may refer to different nodes.
Snaking prose uses d_h=15 while code constructs open candidates at sepdist*1.5 after initializing sepdist=10; the parameter link is implicit and brittle.
Several quadrant formulas and a branch using rep(1,1) instead of the latest repeater make the direction computation difficult to reconcile with Algorithm 2.
Boundary fallback repeatedly changes angles but does not visibly enforce a safe candidate-index or retry bound.
Branching runs kmeans on concat containing x, y, and density score, whereas the paper describes geographic x-y clustering; scale normalization is not supplied.
Branching initializes cluslongscr with numclus rows but loops over numlongdist clusters, relying on implicit array growth and inconsistent dimensions.
The nearest-neighbor long-distance CTCSS chain and indexnum==actlongdist boundary logic are heuristic and may mishandle cycle completion or self-selection.
Branching appears to index pluncovered(i) as a scalar where two coordinate columns are needed, indicating a likely coordinate bug.
Large blocks of source code are commented out with percent-brace delimiters, include debugging output and hard-coded alternatives, and do not establish which path generated the published figures.
Multiple long MATLAB lines are physically cropped at the right page edge, so parts of conditions and plotting calls cannot be recovered from either text extraction or raster review.
